Authors Affiliation * 1 School of Environmental Science & Engineering, Shanghai Jiaotong University, 800 Dongchuan Avenue, Shanghai 200240, People's Republic China. * PMID: 15881029 * DOI: 10.1080/09593332608618563 Abstract Batch and semi-continuous experiments were carried out to determine the effect of pH on hydrolysis and acidogenesis of kitchen wastes in the two-phase anaerobic digestion. The results of the batch experiment showed pH adjustment could improve both hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates of kitchen wastes. Compared with pH at 5, 9 and 11, pH 7 provided an optimum working condition for anaerobic digestion of kitchen wastes. At pH 7, about 86% of the total organic carbon (TOC) and 82% of chemical oxygen demand (COD) were solubilized and the maximum volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentration of 36 g l(-1) was achieved on the fourth day. The total VFA yield was 0.27 g (g total solid (TS))(-1), which almost doubled the yield without pH adjustment (0.15 g (g TS)(-1). The acidified products with lower concentration of lactic acid were more favorable to the subsequent methanogenesis. At pH 7, most of the protein was degraded into ammonia nitrogen (NH4(+)-N), resulting in additional buffer of acidified liquid. According to this, a novel method of pH adjustment applying NH4(+)-N buffer was established. The semi-continuous experiment indicated that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage in the two-phase anaerobic digestion process would increase both TS loading rate (16g l(-1) d(-1)) and recovery of biological energy (520 ml methane (CH4) (g TS)(-1)). fetched_contents.text: Post-treatment of dewatered digested sewage sludge by thermophilic high-solid digestion for pasteurization with positive energy output Highlights * • Thermophilic dry digestion of DDS increases methane yield by 6% * • Thermophilic dry digestion of DDS at 52 °C efficiently converts organic N. * • Thermophilic dry digestion of DDS is stable at high free ammonia levels (2 g/L) * • Increasing ammonia level enriches members of the methanogenic family WSA2. * • Sanitization of DDS by thermophilic dry digestion has a positive energy balance. Abstract This study investigated the possibility to use thermophilic anaerobic high solid digestion of dewatered digested sewage sludge (DDS) at a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) as a measure to increase total methane yield, achieve pasteurization and reduce risk for methane emissions during storage of the digestate. A pilot-scale plug-flow reactor was used to mimic thermophilic post-treatment of DDS from a WWTP in Linköping, Sweden. Process operation was evaluated with respect to biogas process performance, using both chemical and microbiological parameters. Initially, the process showed disturbance, with low methane yields and high volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation. However, after initiation of digestate recirculation performance improved and the specific methane production reached 46 mL CH4/g VS. Plug flow conditions were assessed with lithium chloride and the hydraulic retention time (HRT) was determined to be 19–29 days, sufficient to reach successful pasteurization. Degradation rate of raw protein was high and resulted in ammonia-nitrogen levels of up to 2.0 g/L and a 30% lower protein content in the digestate as compared to DDS. Microbial analysis suggested a shift in the methane producing pathway, with dominance of syntrophic acetate oxidation and the candidate methanogen family WSA2 by the end of the experiment. Energy balance calculations based on annual DDS production of 10 000 ton/year showed that introduction of high-solid digestion as a post-treatment and pasteurization method would result in a positive energy output of 340 MWh/year. Post-digestion of DDS also decreased residual methane potential (RMP) by>96% compared with fresh DDS. Introduction Anaerobic digestion (AD) of sewage sludge is a commonly applied approach to stabilize sewage sludge and simultaneously produce biogas. In 2017, 753 GWh of biogas were produced at Swedish wastewater treatment plants (WWTP), representing 36% of all biogas produced in Sweden, with the remainder deriving from food waste, slaughterhouse waste, and other industrial wastes (SwedishEnergyAgency, 2018). This represented an increase of 6% compared with the previous year (SwedishEnergyAgency, 2018). Biogas produced at WWTP plants is often used for generation of electricity and heat and can supply a substantial proportion of the energy used at the treatment plant (Jenicek et al., 2012). In addition, the biogas can be used as vehicle fuel after upgrading (normally > 97% methane content) (SiS, 1999). This is common practice in Sweden (SwedishEnergyAgency, 2018), with 65% of all biogas produced at WWTPs in 2017 being upgraded to vehicle fuel (Energimyndigheten, 2017). Increased production and upgrading of biogas at WWTPs is one important step in reaching Sweden’s target of a fossil-free vehicle fleet by 2030. In addition to biogas, AD results in a nutrient-rich digestate that can be used as a fertilizer in agriculture (Arthurson, 2009, Nkoa, 2013). In 2017, >2.7 million metric tons of digestate were produced in Sweden, of which 83% were used as fertilizer. Of the digestate produced at WWTPs in that year, 31% (187 kton) was used as agricultural fertilizer (Energimyndigheten, 2017). The use of digestate from biogas plants in Sweden is regulated by two different certification systems, one for digestates from WWTPs (Revaq) and one for plants operating with other organic materials, often in co-digestion (Sweden, 2013). Both systems require e.g., analysis of indicator pathogens, metal concentrations, visible impurities, and nutrient levels. In addition, biogas plants operating with animal-based waste are obliged to use a pasteurization step for use of the digestate as a fertilizer. These regulations are set by European Union (EU) regulations (EG) no. 1069/2009 and (EU) no. 142/2011) to avoid spread of pathogens, such as enterococci or salmonella. These regulations currently does not apply to sludge from WWTPs. However, the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency has proposed new directives that will make it mandatory to pasteurize all sludge from WWTPs (Naturvårdsverket, 2013). Consequently, stabilization by storage for 6 months, as used today, will not be allowed for sewage sludge in the future. If the new regulations come into force, major changes may be needed to meet the pasteurization requirement at many WWTP plants in Sweden. There are several common methods for pasteurization of sludge (and other biomass types) at biogas plants. The most common method in Sweden is heating at ≥ 70 °C for 1 h (prior or post digestion) (Bagge et al., 2005). In addition, applying a thermophilic digestion temperature of 52 and 55 °C can be used, with a exposure time of at least 24 and 8 h, respectively (Naturvårdsverket, 2013). fetched_contents.text: Post-hydrolysis versus side-stream ammonia stripping in semi-continuous two-stage anaerobic digestion of high nitrogen feedstock Introduction Anaerobic Digestion (AD) is an established organic waste management technology that unlocks the value of wastes and converts them into valuable products, biogas and fertilizers (Baldi et al., 2018, Jain et al., 2015). As biogas production from organic waste material is gaining more ground worldwide as a means to produce sustainable bioenergy, research advancements focus on increasing the inclusivity of biogas reactors to treat a wider range of organic wastes that may encounter issues during digestion. One such issue is ammonia toxicity during the AD of poultry manure (PM), which has excluded PM as a primary biogas feedstock unless it was diluted or subjected to extremely long retention times to allow acclimation of microbes to high ammonia levels (Rajagopal et al., 2013a, Wang et al., 2016, Zhu et al., 2022). Ammonia stripping is the most commonly used technique to address ammonia toxicity in AD operation due to its relatively simple concept, applicability at large scales, and manageable economics (Bi et al., 2020, Fuchs et al., 2018, Yellezuome et al., 2022). Ammonia stripping of digestate is operated under high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility and improve the removal efficiency (Li et al., 2018, Serna-Maza et al., 2014). Recent studies have been concerned with optimizing the process by examining different aspects, specifically the stage at which the stripping is implemented and the type of stripping gas. In a two-stage AD operation, the ammonia stripping could be implemented either as Post-hydrolysis Ammonia Stripping (PHAS) or Side-stream Ammonia Stripping (SSAS). In PHAS configuration, ammonia stripping is conducted at an intermediate stage between the hydrolysis and methanogenesis phases, where ammonia fermentation is mostly completed (Huang et al., 2019, Walker et al., 2011). On the other hand, SSAS includes stripping a portion of the digester's volume (typically 2–5% per day) in a side column and returning the ammonia-stripped digestate to the main AD reactor to reduce ammonia levels (Li et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2017). Both PHAS and SSAS systems operate at significantly different ammonia stripping tower conditions. For example, SSAS is often conducted using biogas recirculation, which can severely impact the buffering capacity of the material and reduce the ammonia removal efficiency. Therefore, biogas recirculation is often conducted at a very low flow rate (1–10 L biogas/ L/ hour) and relies on high volatility of ammonia at a pH level above 10, temperatures above 65 °C, and long durations of more than 24 h (Li et al., 2018, Serna-Maza et al., 2014). On the other hand, PHAS systems provide more flexibility in selecting stripping gas and can be conducted using air, which has a high removal efficiency and low impact on the buffering capacity of the material (Bousek et al., 2016). Thus, systems with air stripping can operate under pH levels of 9–10, temperatures of 40–55 °C, and durations of 1–4 h (Fakkaew and Polprasert, 2021, Huang et al., 2019). There is very limited information in the literature regarding the performance of PHAS and SSAS, and the comparison of their performance under similar testing conditions. Huang et al. (2019) was the only study to experimentally test the performance of PHAS of swine manure at a high solid content of 25% and observed a 60–70% improvement in biogas production. However, the results were limited to batch testing; there are no studies that covered the continuous or semi-continuous operations of PHAS. Serna-Maza et al., 2014, Zhang et al., 2017 reported that the SSAS system successfully alleviated ammonia inhibition in the thermophilic digestion of food waste in a semi-continuous mode. Yin et al. (2019) investigated hyper-thermophilic ammonia stripping in an in-situ configuration similar to SSAS with biogas recirculation and its effect on the efficiency of different AD phases and biogas production. The study found that increasing organic loading rate (OLR) and decreasing hydraulic retention time (HRT) can increase ammonia levels to inhibitory levels (2500–3000 mg NH3-N/L) and reduce biogas production by 75% even when ammonia stripping was still implemented. Walker et al. (2011) was the only study to compare the performance of different configurations of ammonia stripping from source-segregated food waste based on kinetic modelling. They reported that the PHAS system was more advantageous than SSAS because it resulted in higher methane production and lower ammonia levels in the digestate. However, they stated that their conclusions were limited to modelling alone due to the lack of experimental data, specifically on the PHAS system. Considering the above, there is an insisting need to compare the ammonia stripping configurations to identify the advantages and disadvantages of each system over the other. In previous studies by the authors (Adghim et al., 2022, Adghim et al., 2021), the PHAS system was investigated for the mono- and co-digestion of PM in batch mode, and the stripping conditions were optimized at pH 9.5, temperature of 55 °C, and gas flowrate of 100 L gas/L/ hr. Furthermore, the feasibility of using renewable natural gas (RNG) as a stripping gas was investigated in PHAS, which yielded promising results and comparable performance to the application of air in terms of ammonia removal efficiency (60–70%) and biogas production enhancement (65–80%) in batch mode. However, assessing the PHAS under continuous long-term operation and its comparison with the SSAS process is yet to be evaluated (Adghim et al., 2023). As RNG is a valuable product of biogas plants, it is important to note that RNG used in stripping columns must be recycled after passing through an ammonia trap instead of using fresh RNG for the stripping. Mechanistic explanation of how acidic post-treatments enhance methane production

Acidic post-treatments enhance methane production by accelerating the early anaerobic digestion stages and altering the microbial environment in ways that favor acidogenesis over methanogenesis. The evidence base here is centered on pH effects on hydrolysis and acidogenesis, and on how these changes can indirectly support downstream methane yield. A key study on kitchen waste in two-phase anaerobic digestion found that pH adjustment improved both hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, with pH 7 identified as an optimum condition for anaerobic digestion. At pH 7, about 86% of total organic carbon and 82% of chemical oxygen demand were solubilized, and volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentration reached 36 g/L on the fourth day; the total VFA yield was 0.27 g per g total solid, almost doubling the yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. This suggests that a mildly acidic or neutral pH can optimize the breakdown of complex organic matter into soluble substrates and short-chain fatty acids, which are then available for acidogenic fermentation.

The broader anaerobic digestion process structure also supports this mechanism. The four-phase model describes hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis, with acidogenesis producing volatile fatty acids and other soluble organic intermediates that feed acetogenesis and eventually methanogenesis [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. Acidic post-treatment therefore appears to shorten or intensify the acidogenic phase by increasing the availability of substrates, while also influencing microbial community activity. In the kitchen-waste study, pH adjustment was associated with a lower concentration of lactic acid in the acidified products and a shift toward more favorable conditions for subsequent methanogenesis [N1-F1]. This implies that acidic treatment can improve the quality of the acidogenic products, reducing inhibitory byproducts and creating a more methanogenic-friendly environment downstream.

Volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release are central to this mechanism. The kitchen-waste study showed a substantial increase in soluble organic matter release at pH 7, with significant solubilization of TOC and COD and a marked rise in VFA concentration [N1-F1]. The evidence also links this release to higher subsequent methane production: the semi-continuous experiment found that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. This indicates that acidic post-treatment enhances methane production not only by accelerating acidogenesis, but also by increasing the quantity and quality of soluble organic matter available for further microbial conversion.

A major caveat is the potential for methanogen inhibition versus acidogen stimulation. The evidence does not explicitly state that methanogens are stimulated by acidic post-treatment, but it does show that low pH can alter microbial community activity in ways that improve digestion outcomes. In the kitchen-waste study, the acidified products were described as more favorable to subsequent methanogenesis, suggesting that the acidic phase itself may buffer or reduce the negative effects of acid accumulation rather than directly stimulating methanogens [N1-F1]. In contrast, other sources emphasize that ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis can reduce ammonia toxicity, which is important because high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may work best when it is paired with measures to manage ammonia or when it is used in a system where the microbial community is adapted to the pH shift.

In summary, acidic post-treatments enhance methane production by accelerating hydrolysis and acidogenesis, increasing soluble organic matter and VFA release, and creating acidogenic products that are more favorable to downstream methanogenesis. However, the evidence also suggests that the effect depends on maintaining a balance: low pH can stimulate acidogens and improve substrate availability, but it may also impose stress on methanogens if ammonia or other inhibitors are not managed [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4].

Operational factors determining treatment effectiveness

The effectiveness of acidic treatments depends on a combination of pH, temperature, retention time, digestate composition, and pretreatment history. The evidence indicates that optimal conditions are not necessarily extreme acidity; instead, pH adjustment appears to be most beneficial when it is tailored to the digestate and digestion phase. In the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, pH 7 was identified as the optimum condition for anaerobic digestion, with improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates [N1-F1]. This suggests that acidic post-treatment may be most effective within a narrow pH range that supports both acidogenesis and subsequent methanogenesis, rather than at strongly acidic pHs that could inhibit microbial activity.

Temperature and retention time are also critical. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies shows that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This is important because acidic post-treatment may require careful control of temperature and retention time to avoid stressing the microbial community. In the kitchen-waste study, the process was evaluated in both batch and semi-continuous experiments, and the semi-continuous results showed improved performance when pH was adjusted to 7 in the acidogenic stage [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that longer retention times can be beneficial for acidogenesis and VFA accumulation, but that too-long retention times can lead to instability or excessive inhibition [N1-F1]. The broader anaerobic digestion literature notes that process indicators such as volatile fatty acids, alkalinity ratio, and redox potential are key to process control [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that operational factors must be monitored closely.

Digestate composition has a major impact on treatment response. The kitchen-waste study showed that pH adjustment increased solubilization of total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand, with a total VFA yield of 0.27 g per g total solid [N1-F1]. This suggests that digestate with a higher proportion of recalcitrant or insoluble organic matter may respond more strongly to acidic pretreatment. The digestate composition evidence also highlights the importance of nitrogen content and ammonia dynamics. In the context of anaerobic digestion, digestate is described as nutrient-rich, containing up to 20% solids and significant amounts of nutrients [N6-R2]. Pretreatment literature indicates that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structures and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1], while ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis can alter ammonia content and reduce toxicity [N5-F3], [N7-R1]. These findings imply that digestate with high solids content, high organic fraction, or high ammonia levels may behave differently under acidic treatment, and that pretreatment can be used to make the digestate more responsive.

Pretreatment history is another key determinant of response to acidic treatment. The evidence on digestate pretreatment shows that liquid pretreatment can improve solubilization and anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1], while pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can change digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content [N4-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. This means that a digestate that has already undergone pretreatment may have a different response to acidic post-treatment. For example, pretreatment may already have reduced solids content or increased solubility, which can make further acidic treatment more effective [N4-R1]. Conversely, pretreatment may also alter the microbial community or buffering capacity, which could either enhance or hinder the acidic post-treatment effect [N4-R1], [N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can affect ammonia levels, which is important because high ammonia can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Thus, pretreatment history can fundamentally change whether acidic post-treatment is beneficial, neutral, or potentially harmful.

In practical terms, the most effective acidic treatments are likely to occur in systems where pH is adjusted to a mild or neutral optimum, temperature and retention time are managed to avoid methanogen stress, and digestate composition is favorable for solubilization and VFA release. Pretreatment history should therefore be considered as a prior condition that can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N6-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4].

Digestate pretreatment effects and post-treatment interactions

Pretreatment changes digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content in ways that can strongly influence the response to subsequent acidic treatment. The evidence shows that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structure and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. This structural disruption likely increases solubility, making more organic matter available for microbial conversion. The acidic pretreatment evidence similarly indicates that acidic pretreatment can disrupt recalcitrant features of organic materials and make them accessible for further processing [N4-R2]. In the context of digestate, this means that prior pretreatment can already reduce the need for intense acidic post-treatment by increasing solubility and reducing recalcitrance [N4-R1], [N4-R2].

Ammonia content is another major pretreatment-related factor. The evidence on ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis shows that pretreatment can alter ammonia levels and improve ammonia removal efficiency [N5-F3], [N7-R1], [N7-R2]. In particular, thermal hydrolysis pretreatment upstream of anaerobic digestion is used to improve AD efficiency, and ammonia stripping is commonly used to address ammonia toxicity [N7-R2], [N7-R5]. This is important because ammonia is a key inhibitor of methanogens, and high ammonia levels can reduce methane yield [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. If digestate has already been pretreated to lower ammonia content or to release ammonia more effectively, the subsequent acidic treatment may be less stressful for the microbial community. Conversely, if pretreatment leaves the digestate with high ammonia or buffering capacity, acidic treatment could be more challenging.

Pretreatment can make or hinder subsequent acidic treatment depending on the specific strategy. The evidence indicates that pretreatment can be beneficial by improving solubility and reducing recalcitrance [N4-R1], [N4-R2]. However, it can also create trade-offs. For example, pretreatment may alter the microbial community, buffering capacity, or nutrient composition, which could either enhance or impair the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N7-R2]. Pretreatment may also change the digestate’s solids content and organic fraction, which are relevant to acidic treatment effectiveness [N6-R2]. The evidence further shows that pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can improve AD efficiency, but that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility [N5-F3]. This suggests that some pretreatment strategies may create conditions that are less compatible with acidic post-treatment, especially if they are designed to operate at high pH or high temperature [N5-F3].

Examples of pretreatment strategies and their compatibility with acid post-treatment are important. Liquid pretreatment is clearly compatible because it can improve digestate structure and solubility [N4-R1]. Ammonia stripping is compatible in the sense that it reduces ammonia toxicity, which is important for maintaining methanogen activity [N5-F3], [N7-R1], [N8-R2]. Thermal hydrolysis is compatible with anaerobic digestion optimization, but its main role is often upstream of digestion rather than as a direct acid post-treatment [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can be used to make digestate more responsive to acidic treatment by reducing recalcitrance and improving solubility, but it can also create conditions where acidic post-treatment is more challenging if ammonia or buffering capacity remains high [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N5-F3]. Overall, the most compatible pretreatment strategies are those that improve digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia management, while minimizing adverse changes to the microbial environment [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

Evidence base and practical context for acidic post-treatment use

The evidence base for acidic post-treatment use is mixed but suggestive. Direct evidence on acidic treatment comes from the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, which showed that pH adjustment improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, increased soluble organic matter and VFA release, and almost doubled VFA yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. The study also reported that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that acidic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but only under carefully controlled conditions.

The evidence also shows that acidic post-treatment can be part of a broader post-treatment strategy. The kitchen-waste study is specifically about pH adjustment during digestion, rather than a separate post-treatment step, so it is more a demonstration of pH control than a pure post-treatment example. In contrast, the post-treatment literature includes studies on thermophilic high-solid digestion of dewatered digested sewage sludge, which reported a 6% increase in methane yield and efficient conversion of organic nitrogen, with high free ammonia levels tolerated in the system [N3-F2]. This suggests that acidic or thermophilic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but the exact role of acidity is not the central focus of that study. Still, it demonstrates that post-treatment can be used to increase methane yield and meet operational goals such as pasteurization [N3-F2].

In terms of limitations and side effects, the evidence indicates that acidic conditions can impose stress on the microbial community. The literature on ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis notes that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility, which can affect buffering capacity and reduce ammonia removal efficiency if biogas recirculation is used [N5-F3]. In addition, other sources state that high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens and that aceticlastic methanogenesis is more sensitive to ammonia than hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic methanogenesis [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may need to be paired with ammonia management or adapted to avoid methanogen inhibition. The kitchen-waste study also shows that the acidified products were more favorable to subsequent methanogenesis, but the evidence does not explicitly state that acidic treatment itself stimulates methanogens; rather, it suggests that the acidogenic phase can be optimized to produce better feedstock for methanogenesis [N1-F1].

Operational trade-offs are also important. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies indicates that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This means that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature, retention time, and pH control. The evidence also shows that pretreatment can alter digestate composition and ammonia content, which can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. In practical terms, acidic post-treatment may be most effective when it is used as a controlled phase adjustment rather than a harsh acidification step, and when it is combined with measures to manage ammonia or improve microbial resilience.

When compared with other post-treatment strategies, acidic post-treatment sits between pH control and more intensive physicochemical treatments. Ammonia stripping is often used to address ammonia toxicity, and the evidence shows that post-hydrolysis ammonia stripping can be a favorable ammonia-targeted treatment, achieving higher methane potential than side-stream stripping in some cases [N5-F3]. Thermal hydrolysis is another common post-treatment strategy that improves AD efficiency by enhancing ammonia release and solubilizing organic matter [N5-F3], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. In contrast, acidic post-treatment appears to focus more on optimizing acidogenesis and VFA release rather than on ammonia stripping or thermal disruption [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that acidic post-treatment can be a useful strategy in systems where pH adjustment can improve hydrolysis and acidogenesis, but it is less clearly established as a standalone replacement for ammonia stripping or thermal hydrolysis [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

In conclusion, the evidence base supports the idea that acidic post-treatment can enhance methane yield by improving hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and soluble organic matter release, but it is limited in scope and often studied as pH control rather than a pure post-treatment step [N1-F1]. The main practical context is that acidic post-treatment should be used within a controlled operational framework, with attention to pH, ammonia, temperature, and retention time, and that it may be most compatible with pretreatment strategies that improve digestate solubility and ammonia management [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. Compared with other post-treatment strategies, it is less about extreme physical or chemical disruption and more about optimizing the early digestion phases [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

## How acidic post-treatments enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate

Acidic post-treatments can enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate by accelerating the early anaerobic digestion stages and improving the availability of substrates for microbial conversion. The mechanism is not simply direct stimulation of methanogens under low pH, but rather a combination of improved hydrolysis, increased acidogenesis, and better acidogenic product quality that supports downstream methanogenesis. The kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study provides a direct example: pH adjustment improved both hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, with pH 7 identified as an optimal condition for anaerobic digestion [N1-F1]. At pH 7, about 86% of total organic carbon and 82% of chemical oxygen demand were solubilized, and volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentration reached 36 g/L on the fourth day; the total VFA yield was 0.27 g per g total solid, almost doubling the yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. This indicates that acidic post-treatment can increase the quantity and quality of soluble organic matter and VFA release, which are important substrates for further microbial conversion [N1-F1], [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5].

## Mechanisms by which acidic post-treatments enhance methane production

### Low pH affects hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and microbial community activity
Acidic post-treatments work by altering the pH environment in a way that can favor acidogenesis over methanogenesis in the early digestion stages. In the kitchen-waste study, pH adjustment was associated with lower lactic acid concentrations in the acidified products and more favorable conditions for subsequent methanogenesis [N1-F1]. This suggests that acidic treatment can reduce inhibitory acid accumulation and create a better feedstock for the later methanogenic phase [N1-F1]. The broader anaerobic digestion framework also supports this: the process is divided into hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis, with acidogenesis producing volatile fatty acids and other soluble intermediates that feed acetogenesis and eventually methanogenesis [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. So, acidic post-treatment appears to speed up or intensify the acidogenic phase, while also influencing microbial community activity in a way that improves digestion outcomes [N1-F1].

### Role of volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release
Volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release are central to the mechanism. ## What factors influence the effectiveness of acidic post-treatment?

### Optimal pH, temperature, and retention time ranges
The effectiveness of acidic treatment depends on a carefully balanced operating regime. The evidence indicates that pH 7 was optimal for anaerobic digestion of kitchen waste, with improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates [N1-F1]. This suggests that acidic post-treatment is most effective within a narrow pH range that supports both acidogenesis and subsequent methanogenesis, rather than at strongly acidic pHs that could inhibit microbial activity [N1-F1]. Temperature and retention time are also critical. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies shows that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This implies that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature and retention time to avoid stressing the microbial community [N2-R5]. The broader anaerobic digestion literature notes that process indicators such as volatile fatty acids, alkalinity ratio, and redox potential are key to process control [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that operational factors must be monitored closely.

Digestate composition strongly influences the response to acidic treatment. The kitchen-waste study showed that pH adjustment increased solubilization of total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand, with a total VFA yield of 0.27 g per g total solid [N1-F1]. This suggests that digestate with a higher proportion of recalcitrant or insoluble organic matter may respond more strongly to acidic pretreatment. Digestate is typically nutrient-rich and may contain up to 20% solids [N6-R2]. Pretreatment literature also indicates that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structures and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. This implies that digestate with high solids content, high organic fraction, or high recalcitrance may behave differently under acidic treatment, and that pretreatment can be used to make the digestate more responsive [N4-R1], [N6-R2].

### Pretreatment history and how it alters response to acid treatment
Pretreatment history is another major determinant of response to acidic treatment. The evidence on digestate pretreatment shows that liquid pretreatment can improve solubilization and anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. It also indicates that pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can change digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content [N4-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. This means that a digestate that has already undergone pretreatment may have a different response to acidic post-treatment. For example, pretreatment may already have reduced solids content or increased solubility, which can make further acidic treatment more effective [N4-R1]. Conversely, pretreatment may also alter the microbial community, buffering capacity, or nutrient composition, which could either enhance or hinder the acidic post-treatment effect [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can affect ammonia levels, which is important because high ammonia can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Thus, pretreatment history can fundamentally change whether acidic post-treatment is beneficial, neutral, or potentially harmful [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N6-R2], [N7-R2].

## Evidence base and practical context for acidic post-treatment use

The evidence base for acidic post-treatment is mixed but suggestive. Direct evidence on acidic treatment comes from the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, which showed that pH adjustment improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, increased soluble organic matter and VFA release, and almost doubled VFA yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. The study also reported that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that acidic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but only under carefully controlled conditions.

In practical terms, acidic post-treatment should be viewed as part of a broader operational framework rather than a standalone high-acid treatment. The kitchen-waste study is specifically about pH adjustment during digestion, rather than a separate post-treatment step, so it is more a demonstration of pH control than a pure post-treatment example [N1-F1]. In contrast, the post-treatment literature includes studies on thermophilic high-solid digestion of dewatered digested sewage sludge, which reported a 6% increase in methane yield and efficient conversion of organic nitrogen, with high free ammonia levels tolerated in the system [N3-F2]. This suggests that post-treatment can be used to increase methane yield and meet operational goals such as pasteurization [N3-F2]. However, the exact role of acidity in that study is not the central focus, so it is less directly comparable to acidic post-treatment as a pure pH-driven strategy [N3-F2].

## Limitations, side effects, and operational trade-offs

The main limitations and side effects of acidic post-treatment are related to microbial inhibition, ammonia toxicity, and operational control. The evidence indicates that ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis are used to address ammonia toxicity, and that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility [N5-F3]. In addition, other sources state that high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens and that aceticlastic methanogenesis is more sensitive to ammonia than hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic methanogenesis [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may need to be paired with ammonia management or adapted to avoid methanogen inhibition. Operational trade-offs are also important. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies indicates that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This means that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature, retention time, and pH control [N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that pretreatment can alter digestate composition and ammonia content, which can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. In practical terms, acidic post-treatment may be most effective when it is used as a controlled phase adjustment rather than a harsh acidification step, and when it is combined with measures to manage ammonia or improve microbial resilience [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

## How acidic treatment compares with other post-treatment strategies

Acidic post-treatment sits between pH control and more intensive physicochemical treatments. Ammonia stripping is often used to address ammonia toxicity, and the evidence shows that post-hydrolysis ammonia stripping can be a favorable ammonia-targeted treatment, achieving higher methane potential than side-stream stripping in some cases [N5-F3]. Thermal hydrolysis is another common post-treatment strategy that improves AD efficiency by enhancing ammonia release and solubilizing organic matter [N5-F3], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. In contrast, acidic post-treatment appears to focus more on optimizing acidogenesis and VFA release rather than on ammonia stripping or thermal disruption [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that acidic post-treatment can be a useful strategy in systems where pH adjustment can improve hydrolysis and acidogenesis, but it is less clearly established as a standalone replacement for ammonia stripping or thermal hydrolysis [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

## Practical conclusions

Overall, acidic post-treatments can enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate by accelerating hydrolysis and acidogenesis, increasing soluble organic matter and VFA release, and creating acidogenic products that are more favorable to downstream methanogenesis [N1-F1], [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. Pretreatment changes digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content in ways that can strongly influence the response to subsequent acidic treatment. The evidence shows that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structure and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. Ammonia content is another major pretreatment-related factor. Pretreatment can make or hinder subsequent acidic treatment depending on the specific strategy. Evidence base and practical context for acidic post-treatment use

The evidence base for acidic post-treatment use is mixed but suggestive. Direct evidence on acidic treatment comes from the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, which showed that pH adjustment improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, increased soluble organic matter and VFA release, and almost doubled VFA yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. The study also reported that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that acidic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but only under carefully controlled conditions.

The evidence also shows that acidic post-treatment can be part of a broader post-treatment strategy. The kitchen-waste study is specifically about pH adjustment during digestion, rather than a separate post-treatment step, so it is more a demonstration of pH control than a pure post-treatment example. In contrast, the post-treatment literature includes studies on thermophilic high-solid digestion of dewatered digested sewage sludge, which reported a 6% increase in methane yield and efficient conversion of organic nitrogen, with high free ammonia levels tolerated in the system [N3-F2]. This suggests that acidic or thermophilic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but the exact role of acidity is not the central focus of that study. Still, it demonstrates that post-treatment can be used to increase methane yield and meet operational goals such as pasteurization [N3-F2].

In terms of limitations and side effects, the evidence indicates that acidic conditions can impose stress on the microbial community. The literature on ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis notes that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility, which can affect buffering capacity and reduce ammonia removal efficiency if biogas recirculation is used [N5-F3]. In addition, other sources state that high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens and that aceticlastic methanogenesis is more sensitive to ammonia than hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic methanogenesis [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may need to be paired with ammonia management or adapted to avoid methanogen inhibition. The kitchen-waste study also shows that the acidified products were more favorable to subsequent methanogenesis, but the evidence does not explicitly state that acidic treatment itself stimulates methanogens; rather, it suggests that the acidogenic phase can be optimized to produce better feedstock for methanogenesis [N1-F1].

Operational trade-offs are also important. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies indicates that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This means that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature, retention time, and pH control. The evidence also shows that pretreatment can alter digestate composition and ammonia content, which can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. In practical terms, acidic post-treatment may be most effective when it is used as a controlled phase adjustment rather than a harsh acidification step, and when it is combined with measures to manage ammonia or improve microbial resilience.

When compared with other post-treatment strategies, acidic post-treatment sits between pH control and more intensive physicochemical treatments. Ammonia stripping is often used to address ammonia toxicity, and the evidence shows that post-hydrolysis ammonia stripping can be a favorable ammonia-targeted treatment, achieving higher methane potential than side-stream stripping in some cases [N5-F3]. Thermal hydrolysis is another common post-treatment strategy that improves AD efficiency by enhancing ammonia release and solubilizing organic matter [N5-F3], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. In contrast, acidic post-treatment appears to focus more on optimizing acidogenesis and VFA release rather than on ammonia stripping or thermal disruption [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that acidic post-treatment can be a useful strategy in systems where pH adjustment can improve hydrolysis and acidogenesis, but it is less clearly established as a standalone replacement for ammonia stripping or thermal hydrolysis [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

In conclusion, the evidence base supports the idea that acidic post-treatment can enhance methane yield by improving hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and soluble organic matter release, but it is limited in scope and often studied as pH control rather than a pure post-treatment step [N1-F1]. The main practical context is that acidic post-treatment should be used within a controlled operational framework, with attention to pH, ammonia, temperature, and retention time, and that it may be most compatible with pretreatment strategies that improve digestate solubility and ammonia management [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. Compared with other post-treatment strategies, it is less about extreme physical or chemical disruption and more about optimizing the early digestion phases [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

## How acidic post-treatments enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate

Acidic post-treatments can enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate by accelerating the early anaerobic digestion stages and improving the availability of substrates for microbial conversion. The mechanism is not simply direct stimulation of methanogens under low pH, but rather a combination of improved hydrolysis, increased acidogenesis, and better acidogenic product quality that supports downstream methanogenesis. The kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study provides a direct example: pH adjustment improved both hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, with pH 7 identified as an optimal condition for anaerobic digestion [N1-F1]. At pH 7, about 86% of total organic carbon and 82% of chemical oxygen demand were solubilized, and volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentration reached 36 g/L on the fourth day; the total VFA yield was 0.27 g per g total solid, almost doubling the yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. This indicates that acidic post-treatment can increase the quantity and quality of soluble organic matter and VFA release, which are important substrates for further microbial conversion [N1-F1], [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5].

## Mechanisms by which acidic post-treatments enhance methane production

### Low pH affects hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and microbial community activity
Acidic post-treatments work by altering the pH environment in a way that can favor acidogenesis over methanogenesis in the early digestion stages. In the kitchen-waste study, pH adjustment was associated with lower lactic acid concentrations in the acidified products and more favorable conditions for subsequent methanogenesis [N1-F1]. This suggests that acidic treatment can reduce inhibitory acid accumulation and create a better feedstock for the later methanogenic phase [N1-F1]. The broader anaerobic digestion framework also supports this: the process is divided into hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis, with acidogenesis producing volatile fatty acids and other soluble intermediates that feed acetogenesis and eventually methanogenesis [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. So, acidic post-treatment appears to speed up or intensify the acidogenic phase, while also influencing microbial community activity in a way that improves digestion outcomes [N1-F1].

### Role of volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release
Volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release are central to the mechanism. The kitchen-waste study showed substantial increases in soluble organic matter release at pH 7, with significant solubilization of total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand and a marked rise in VFA concentration [N1-F1]. This release of soluble substrates is important because it provides more material for acidogens to convert into shorter-chain organic acids, which can then be used by acetogens and methanogens downstream [N1-F1], [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. The evidence also links this release to higher subsequent methane production: the semi-continuous experiment found that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. Thus, acidic post-treatment enhances methane production not only by accelerating acidogenesis, but also by increasing the quantity and quality of soluble organic matter available for further microbial conversion [N1-F1].

### Potential inhibition of methanogens versus stimulation of acidogens
A key caveat is that acidic post-treatment can impose stress on methanogens if not managed carefully. The evidence shows that ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis are used to address ammonia toxicity, and that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility [N5-F3]. In addition, other sources emphasize that high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens and that aceticlastic methanogenesis is more sensitive to ammonia than hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic methanogenesis [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may work best when it is paired with measures to manage ammonia or when it is used in a system where the microbial community is adapted to the pH shift. In other words, acidic post-treatment may stimulate acidogens and improve acidogenesis, but it may also stress methanogens if ammonia or other inhibitors are not controlled [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4].

Temperature and retention time are also critical. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies shows that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This implies that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature and retention time to avoid stressing the microbial community [N2-R5]. The broader anaerobic digestion literature notes that process indicators such as volatile fatty acids, alkalinity ratio, and redox potential are key to process control [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that operational factors must be monitored closely.

Digestate composition strongly influences the response to acidic treatment. The kitchen-waste study showed that pH adjustment increased solubilization of total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand, with a total VFA yield of 0.27 g per g total solid [N1-F1]. This suggests that digestate with a higher proportion of recalcitrant or insoluble organic matter may respond more strongly to acidic pretreatment. Pretreatment literature also indicates that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structures and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. This implies that digestate with high solids content, high organic fraction, or high recalcitrance may behave differently under acidic treatment, and that pretreatment can be used to make the digestate more responsive [N4-R1], [N6-R2].

Pretreatment history is another major determinant of response to acidic treatment. The evidence on digestate pretreatment shows that liquid pretreatment can improve solubilization and anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. It also indicates that pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can change digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content [N4-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. This means that a digestate that has already undergone pretreatment may have a different response to acidic post-treatment. Conversely, pretreatment may also alter the microbial community, buffering capacity, or nutrient composition, which could either enhance or hinder the acidic post-treatment effect [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can affect ammonia levels, which is important because high ammonia can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. The main limitations and side effects of acidic post-treatment are related to microbial inhibition, ammonia toxicity, and operational control. Overall, acidic post-treatments can enhance methane production from sludge-based digestate by accelerating hydrolysis and acidogenesis, increasing soluble organic matter and VFA release, and creating acidogenic products that are more favorable to downstream methanogenesis [N1-F1], [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. The effectiveness of acidic treatments depends on a combination of pH, temperature, retention time, digestate composition, and pretreatment history. The evidence indicates that optimal conditions are not necessarily extreme acidity; instead, pH adjustment appears to be most beneficial when it is tailored to the digestate and digestion phase. In the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, pH 7 was identified as the optimum condition for anaerobic digestion, with improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates [N1-F1]. This suggests that acidic post-treatment may be most effective within a narrow pH range that supports both acidogenesis and subsequent methanogenesis, rather than at strongly acidic pHs that could inhibit microbial activity.

Temperature and retention time are also critical. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies shows that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This is important because acidic post-treatment may require careful control of temperature and retention time to avoid stressing the microbial community. In the kitchen-waste study, the process was evaluated in both batch and semi-continuous experiments, and the semi-continuous results showed improved performance when pH was adjusted to 7 in the acidogenic stage [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that longer retention times can be beneficial for acidogenesis and VFA accumulation, but that too-long retention times can lead to instability or excessive inhibition [N1-F1]. The broader anaerobic digestion literature notes that process indicators such as volatile fatty acids, alkalinity ratio, and redox potential are key to process control [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that operational factors must be monitored closely.

Digestate composition has a major impact on treatment response. The kitchen-waste study showed that pH adjustment increased solubilization of total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand, with a total VFA yield of 0.27 g per g total solid [N1-F1]. This suggests that digestate with a higher proportion of recalcitrant or insoluble organic matter may respond more strongly to acidic pretreatment. The digestate composition evidence also highlights the importance of nitrogen content and ammonia dynamics. In the context of anaerobic digestion, digestate is described as nutrient-rich, containing up to 20% solids and significant amounts of nutrients [N6-R2]. Pretreatment literature indicates that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structures and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1], while ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis can alter ammonia content and reduce toxicity [N5-F3], [N7-R1]. These findings imply that digestate with high solids content, high organic fraction, or high ammonia levels may behave differently under acidic treatment, and that pretreatment can be used to make the digestate more responsive.

Pretreatment history is another key determinant of response to acidic treatment. The evidence on digestate pretreatment shows that liquid pretreatment can improve solubilization and anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1], while pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can change digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content [N4-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. This means that a digestate that has already undergone pretreatment may have a different response to acidic post-treatment. For example, pretreatment may already have reduced solids content or increased solubility, which can make further acidic treatment more effective [N4-R1]. Conversely, pretreatment may also alter the microbial community or buffering capacity, which could either enhance or hinder the acidic post-treatment effect [N4-R1], [N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can affect ammonia levels, which is important because high ammonia can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Thus, pretreatment history can fundamentally change whether acidic post-treatment is beneficial, neutral, or potentially harmful.

In practical terms, the most effective acidic treatments are likely to occur in systems where pH is adjusted to a mild or neutral optimum, temperature and retention time are managed to avoid methanogen stress, and digestate composition is favorable for solubilization and VFA release. Pretreatment history should therefore be considered as a prior condition that can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N6-R2], [N7-R2], [N7-R4].

Digestate pretreatment effects and post-treatment interactions

Pretreatment changes digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia content in ways that can strongly influence the response to subsequent acidic treatment. The evidence shows that liquid digestate pretreatment can dissolve lignocellulosic structure and promote anaerobic biogas production [N4-R1]. This structural disruption likely increases solubility, making more organic matter available for microbial conversion. The acidic pretreatment evidence similarly indicates that acidic pretreatment can disrupt recalcitrant features of organic materials and make them accessible for further processing [N4-R2]. In the context of digestate, this means that prior pretreatment can already reduce the need for intense acidic post-treatment by increasing solubility and reducing recalcitrance [N4-R1], [N4-R2].

Ammonia content is another major pretreatment-related factor. The evidence on ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis shows that pretreatment can alter ammonia levels and improve ammonia removal efficiency [N5-F3], [N7-R1], [N7-R2]. In particular, thermal hydrolysis pretreatment upstream of anaerobic digestion is used to improve AD efficiency, and ammonia stripping is commonly used to address ammonia toxicity [N7-R2], [N7-R5]. This is important because ammonia is a key inhibitor of methanogens, and high ammonia levels can reduce methane yield [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. If digestate has already been pretreated to lower ammonia content or to release ammonia more effectively, the subsequent acidic treatment may be less stressful for the microbial community. Conversely, if pretreatment leaves the digestate with high ammonia or buffering capacity, acidic treatment could be more challenging.

Pretreatment can make or hinder subsequent acidic treatment depending on the specific strategy. The evidence indicates that pretreatment can be beneficial by improving solubility and reducing recalcitrance [N4-R1], [N4-R2]. However, it can also create trade-offs. For example, pretreatment may alter the microbial community, buffering capacity, or nutrient composition, which could either enhance or impair the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N7-R2]. Pretreatment may also change the digestate’s solids content and organic fraction, which are relevant to acidic treatment effectiveness [N6-R2]. The evidence further shows that pretreatment strategies such as thermal hydrolysis can improve AD efficiency, but that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility [N5-F3]. This suggests that some pretreatment strategies may create conditions that are less compatible with acidic post-treatment, especially if they are designed to operate at high pH or high temperature [N5-F3].

Examples of pretreatment strategies and their compatibility with acid post-treatment are important. Liquid pretreatment is clearly compatible because it can improve digestate structure and solubility [N4-R1]. Ammonia stripping is compatible in the sense that it reduces ammonia toxicity, which is important for maintaining methanogen activity [N5-F3], [N7-R1], [N8-R2]. Thermal hydrolysis is compatible with anaerobic digestion optimization, but its main role is often upstream of digestion rather than as a direct acid post-treatment [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. The evidence also suggests that pretreatment can be used to make digestate more responsive to acidic treatment by reducing recalcitrance and improving solubility, but it can also create conditions where acidic post-treatment is more challenging if ammonia or buffering capacity remains high [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N5-F3]. Overall, the most compatible pretreatment strategies are those that improve digestate structure, solubility, and ammonia management, while minimizing adverse changes to the microbial environment [N4-R1], [N4-R2], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

Evidence base and practical context for acidic post-treatment use

The evidence base for acidic post-treatment use is mixed but suggestive. Direct evidence on acidic treatment comes from the kitchen-waste two-phase anaerobic digestion study, which showed that pH adjustment improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, increased soluble organic matter and VFA release, and almost doubled VFA yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. The study also reported that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that acidic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but only under carefully controlled conditions.

The evidence also shows that acidic post-treatment can be part of a broader post-treatment strategy. The kitchen-waste study is specifically about pH adjustment during digestion, rather than a separate post-treatment step, so it is more a demonstration of pH control than a pure post-treatment example. In contrast, the post-treatment literature includes studies on thermophilic high-solid digestion of dewatered digested sewage sludge, which reported a 6% increase in methane yield and efficient conversion of organic nitrogen, with high free ammonia levels tolerated in the system [N3-F2]. This suggests that acidic or thermophilic post-treatment can improve methane yield, but the exact role of acidity is not the central focus of that study. Still, it demonstrates that post-treatment can be used to increase methane yield and meet operational goals such as pasteurization [N3-F2].

In terms of limitations and side effects, the evidence indicates that acidic conditions can impose stress on the microbial community. The literature on ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis notes that ammonia stripping is often conducted at high pH and temperature to increase ammonia volatility, which can affect buffering capacity and reduce ammonia removal efficiency if biogas recirculation is used [N5-F3]. In addition, other sources state that high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens and that aceticlastic methanogenesis is more sensitive to ammonia than hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic methanogenesis [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may need to be paired with ammonia management or adapted to avoid methanogen inhibition. The kitchen-waste study also shows that the acidified products were more favorable to subsequent methanogenesis, but the evidence does not explicitly state that acidic treatment itself stimulates methanogens; rather, it suggests that the acidogenic phase can be optimized to produce better feedstock for methanogenesis [N1-F1].

Operational trade-offs are also important. The evidence from organic loading rate and retention time studies indicates that short hydraulic retention time and acidic pH can be inhibitory to methanogens [N2-R5]. This means that acidic post-treatment must be implemented with care in terms of temperature, retention time, and pH control. The evidence also shows that pretreatment can alter digestate composition and ammonia content, which can either facilitate or complicate the acidic post-treatment response [N4-R1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. In practical terms, acidic post-treatment may be most effective when it is used as a controlled phase adjustment rather than a harsh acidification step, and when it is combined with measures to manage ammonia or improve microbial resilience.

When compared with other post-treatment strategies, acidic post-treatment sits between pH control and more intensive physicochemical treatments. Ammonia stripping is often used to address ammonia toxicity, and the evidence shows that post-hydrolysis ammonia stripping can be a favorable ammonia-targeted treatment, achieving higher methane potential than side-stream stripping in some cases [N5-F3]. Thermal hydrolysis is another common post-treatment strategy that improves AD efficiency by enhancing ammonia release and solubilizing organic matter [N5-F3], [N7-R2], [N7-R4]. In contrast, acidic post-treatment appears to focus more on optimizing acidogenesis and VFA release rather than on ammonia stripping or thermal disruption [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that acidic post-treatment can be a useful strategy in systems where pH adjustment can improve hydrolysis and acidogenesis, but it is less clearly established as a standalone replacement for ammonia stripping or thermal hydrolysis [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

In conclusion, the evidence base supports the idea that acidic post-treatment can enhance methane yield by improving hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and soluble organic matter release, but it is limited in scope and often studied as pH control rather than a pure post-treatment step [N1-F1]. The main practical context is that acidic post-treatment should be used within a controlled operational framework, with attention to pH, ammonia, temperature, and retention time, and that it may be most compatible with pretreatment strategies that improve digestate solubility and ammonia management [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2]. Compared with other post-treatment strategies, it is less about extreme physical or chemical disruption and more about optimizing the early digestion phases [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N7-R2].

Mechanistic explanation of how acidic post-treatments enhance methane production

Acidic post-treatments enhance methane production by accelerating the early anaerobic digestion stages and altering the microbial environment in ways that favor acidogenesis over methanogenesis. The evidence base here is centered on pH effects on hydrolysis and acidogenesis, and on how these changes can indirectly support downstream methane yield. A key study on kitchen waste in two-phase anaerobic digestion found that pH adjustment improved both hydrolysis and acidogenesis rates, with pH 7 identified as an optimum condition for anaerobic digestion. At pH 7, about 86% of total organic carbon and 82% of chemical oxygen demand were solubilized, and volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentration reached 36 g/L on the fourth day; the total VFA yield was 0.27 g per g total solid, almost doubling the yield without pH adjustment [N1-F1]. This suggests that a mildly acidic or neutral pH can optimize the breakdown of complex organic matter into soluble substrates and short-chain fatty acids, which are then available for acidogenic fermentation.

The broader anaerobic digestion process structure also supports this mechanism. The four-phase model describes hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis, with acidogenesis producing volatile fatty acids and other soluble organic intermediates that feed acetogenesis and eventually methanogenesis [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5]. Acidic post-treatment therefore appears to shorten or intensify the acidogenic phase by increasing the availability of substrates, while also influencing microbial community activity. In the kitchen-waste study, pH adjustment was associated with a lower concentration of lactic acid in the acidified products and a shift toward more favorable conditions for subsequent methanogenesis [N1-F1]. This implies that acidic treatment can improve the quality of the acidogenic products, reducing inhibitory byproducts and creating a more methanogenic-friendly environment downstream.

Volatile fatty acids and soluble organic matter release are central to this mechanism. The kitchen-waste study showed a substantial increase in soluble organic matter release at pH 7, with significant solubilization of TOC and COD and a marked rise in VFA concentration [N1-F1]. The evidence also links this release to higher subsequent methane production: the semi-continuous experiment found that adjusting pH to 7 in the acidogenic stage increased TS loading rate and recovery of biological energy as methane [N1-F1]. This indicates that acidic post-treatment enhances methane production not only by accelerating acidogenesis, but also by increasing the quantity and quality of soluble organic matter available for further microbial conversion.

A major caveat is the potential for methanogen inhibition versus acidogen stimulation. The evidence does not explicitly state that methanogens are stimulated by acidic post-treatment, but it does show that low pH can alter microbial community activity in ways that improve digestion outcomes. In the kitchen-waste study, the acidified products were described as more favorable to subsequent methanogenesis, suggesting that the acidic phase itself may buffer or reduce the negative effects of acid accumulation rather than directly stimulating methanogens [N1-F1]. In contrast, other sources emphasize that ammonia stripping and thermal hydrolysis can reduce ammonia toxicity, which is important because high ammonia levels can inhibit methanogens [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. This implies that acidic post-treatment may work best when it is paired with measures to manage ammonia or when it is used in a system where the microbial community is adapted to the pH shift.

In summary, acidic post-treatments enhance methane production by accelerating hydrolysis and acidogenesis, increasing soluble organic matter and VFA release, and creating acidogenic products that are more favorable to downstream methanogenesis. However, the evidence also suggests that the effect depends on maintaining a balance: low pH can stimulate acidogens and improve substrate availability, but it may also impose stress on methanogens if ammonia or other inhibitors are not managed [N1-F1], [N5-F3], [N8-R2], [N8-R4].
